result.summary: Jupiter calls the gods to witness that the world will perish unless he acts, and strikes Phaëton down with a thunderbolt. The horses bolt and the chariot breaks apart, and Phaëton falls blazing through the sky into the river Eridanus.

scenes.title: Jupiter strikes Phaëton down
scenes.summary: Jupiter calls the gods to witness, climbs to his high vantage point and hurls a lightning bolt that kills Phaëton and quenches the fires.
scenes.stakes: The whole universe will perish in flames unless Jupiter stops the runaway chariot; Phaëton loses his life.

place.name: the highest eminence of the sky

scenes.title: The chariot shatters; Phaëton falls
scenes.summary: The horses break free and the chariot is scattered in pieces. Phaëton falls like a shooting star and the river Eridanus receives him.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton's body is falling in flames; his fall ends in death.

place.name: the air, and the river Eridanus

alias_notes.explanation: A title for Jupiter, father of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid simile comparing Phaëton's blazing fall to a shooting star.

analysis.text: Overreaching ambition ends in catastrophe: Phaëton's attempt to drive the Sun's chariot endangers the world until divine authority restores order.
The episode offers an origin story for natural phenomena such as scorched lands and shooting stars, in the manner of Greek and Roman myth.

legacy.text: Phaëton's fall became a lasting image of reckless ambition and appears in later European art and literature.

fun_facts.text: Ancient writers often identified the Eridanus with the Po in Italy, though the name was also applied to other rivers.

language_notes.text: "Him, too, who had given the chariot" means the Sun, Phaëton's father, whom Jupiter also calls to witness that the world will perish without intervention.
"Eminence" here means a high place or vantage point, the lofty height from which Jupiter works the weather.
"From his right ear" describes Jupiter drawing back the bolt to his ear, like a spear thrower or archer, before hurling it.
"Restrained the flames" means the stronger fire of the thunderbolt put out the fires Phaëton's wild course had kindled.
"Axle-tree" is the axle, the bar on which the wheels turn; "pole" is the shaft to which the horses were yoked.
Eridanus is a river, often identified with the Po in Italy. Phaëton's fall far from his homeland in the east is part of the pathos.

context_notes.text: Jupiter (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and wields thunder and lightning as his weapons.
Phaëton's yellow hair, burning as he falls, makes his death resemble a shooting star.

literary_notes.text: The king of the storm-gods has no clouds or rain left to use, because Phaëton's fire has burned them away. The cause of the crisis disables the usual remedy.
The repeated "in one place... in another" lists the wreckage piece by piece, so the reader sees the chariot's destruction scattered across the scene.
Phaëton's fall is compared to a shooting star, a bright streak across a calm sky. The image makes his death beautiful as well as terrible.
